solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Does it give dairy farmer easy profits?

definitions.text: Does it give dairy farmer easy profits?

parts.words: Does it give dairy farmer easy profits?
parts.note: a business that yields steady money with little effort is named after the animal a dairy farmer milks

explanation.surface: A wondering question about whether dairy farming is an easy route to profit.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally it is a milking animal; the business idiom is a product that reliably earns money for little outlay.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a dependable source of income, pictured as a dairy animal producing milk for its owner.

clue.text: Town decrees filth must be recycled

indicators.note: recycled material is broken down and made into something new, so these letters are reworked into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A council orders the dirt to go off for recycling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must be recycled' rearranges all twelve letters of DECREES FILTH. CHESTERFIELD is a market town in Derbyshire, England, known for its crooked church spire.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterfield is a market town in Derbyshire in the English Midlands.

clue.text: One fielding six balls, in this sweater?

parts.note: in cricket, a slip is a fielder stationed beside the wicketkeeper
in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder wonders whether this jumper is right for standing in the slips during an over.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are cricket terms: a slip is a close fielder behind the batter, and an over is six deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: A slipover is a sleeveless knitted pullover, a kind of jumper pulled on over the head.

clue.text: Start to cut piece of wood, that's around a foot?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of cut is used

parts.note: a log is a cut piece of timber

explanation.surface: Instructions for beginning to cut a piece of wood about a foot long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around a foot' suggests a measurement of twelve inches, but it describes a shoe that encloses the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A clog is a heavy wooden-soled shoe, footwear that wraps around the wearer's foot.

clue.text: Little, almost vile, destructive beetle

parts.note: wee is a Scottish word for small

indicators.note: almost means the word falls one letter short, so the last letter of vile is dropped

explanation.surface: A description of a small, nasty beetle that ruins things.
explanation.definitionFit: A weevil is a small snouted beetle notorious for damaging grain and crops.

clue.text: Shortly notice a piece of ammunition that is found on the beach

indicators.note: shortly means the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: to notice something is to see it
a shell is an explosive artillery projectile

explanation.surface: A warning that a stray piece of ammunition may soon be spotted on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' looks like 'soon' but trims SEE to SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A seashell is the hard outer case of a mollusc, commonly picked up along the shore.

clue.text: After shortening, deliver best part of speech

indicators.note: both words are trimmed, the front of the first and the back of the second cut away, leaving letters that span them

explanation.surface: An instruction to deliver your best speech once it has been cut down.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip DELI from the front of 'deliver' and EST from the end of 'best', and what remains runs across the word gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb is a grammatical word class, one of the traditional parts of speech alongside nouns and adjectives.

clue.text: Always set out for peak

parts.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

indicators.note: out signals the letters of set put out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A mountaineer always setting out for the summit.
explanation.definitionFit: Everest is the highest mountain on Earth, the most famous summit in the Himalayas.

clue.text: Giving place and time immediately

parts.note: there names a place, as opposed to here
then names a time, as opposed to now

explanation.surface: Supplying a location and a date for something to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means at once, on the spot, without delay.

clue.text: One big book on record as a typical example

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece written on another follows it, so the record comes first

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
the Roman numeral I is one
a tome is a large, heavy book

explanation.surface: A big book listed in the record books as a classic case.
explanation.walkthrough: In across answers 'on' puts the later pieces after the record, EP.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is a perfect embodiment or representative instance of a type.

clue.text: Offensive to keep relative in view

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so the relative goes inside the other word

parts.note: vile means foul or offensive
sib is short for sibling, a brother or sister

explanation.surface: An unpleasant relative who stays in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something visible can be seen, so it is within sight.

clue.text: Jog along: revolutionary?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to run at a gentle pace
second meaning: informal short form for a Trotskyist, a follower of the revolutionary Leon Trotsky

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, informal sense: a left-wing radical named after Trotsky.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a slow running pace and a colloquial label for a Trotskyist radical.

clue.text: Partner shows fever after cello playing

indicators.note: the fever comes after the rearranged instrument
playing turns the instrument's letters about, rearranging them

parts.note: ague is an old word for a malarial fever with shivering

explanation.surface: A musical partner comes down with a fever after a cello session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges CELLO to COLLE; ague is an old word for a shivering fever.
explanation.definitionFit: A colleague is a fellow worker, an associate in the same job or profession.

clue.text: To keep small, company dismisses Ukrainians, perhaps

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the small letter goes within the other words

parts.note: to sack someone is to dismiss them from a job
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A firm cutting back to stay small by laying off Ukrainian staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks Ukrainians as an example only, since Cossack communities also lived in southern Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: Cossacks were horsemen of the steppes, many of them from Ukraine, so they illustrate the nationality.

clue.text: I urge man to cultivate a pelargonium

indicators.note: cultivating ground works it over, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Urging a gardener to grow a pelargonium.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelargoniums are popularly called geraniums, the common garden and window-box plant.

clue.text: Anticipate everyone being behind wooded area

indicators.note: the word for everyone is placed behind the woodland, so it comes second

parts.note: a forest is a large wooded area
all means everyone

explanation.surface: Everyone lurking behind a wood, ready to anticipate something.
explanation.definitionFit: To forestall is to act in advance to prevent something, pre-empting it.

clue.text: After a time, crewman is conveniently close

indicators.note: the crewman comes after the a and the time

parts.note: a hand is a crew member on a ship

explanation.surface: A crew member turns up after a while and is handily nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: At hand means nearby and readily available.

clue.text: Plain wicked, swallowing litres

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so the litres go into the other word

parts.note: bad means wicked

explanation.surface: Someone simply wicked, downing litres of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' could be a noun or an adjective here; it is the adjective, meaning unadorned or blunt.
explanation.definitionFit: A bald statement is blunt and unadorned, stated without embellishment.

clue.text: I clean myself, do you hear? Nonsense!

indicators.note: asks the solver to listen, so the phrase is taken by its spoken sound

parts.note: I gives I; to wash is to clean oneself

explanation.surface: An indignant speaker insists on washing themselves and dismisses something as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'I wash' matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is informal for humbug or rubbish, talk meant to deceive.

clue.text: Calm time of day

definitions.meaning: first meaning: level and ...-tempered, as in an ... temper
second meaning: a poetic word for ...

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the literary 'even', short for evening.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means steady or placid and is also an old poetic name for evening.

clue.text: Half a constellation appears pale blue

indicators.note: only half the name is kept, the front four of its eight letters

parts.note: Aquarius, the water carrier, is a constellation of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Part of a star pattern shows up in a light blue colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep the first half of the eight-letter AQUARIUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Aqua is a light greenish-blue colour, named from the Latin for water.

clue.text: As an insignificant person, hard to become PM

parts.note: squit is British slang for a small or contemptible person
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A nobody, with effort, becomes Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: A squit is British slang for a puny nobody. Asquith was British Prime Minister from 1908 to 1916.
explanation.definitionFit: H. H. Asquith was the Liberal Prime Minister of Britain from 1908 to 1916.

clue.text: Do our family make cloth?

parts.note: do becomes does in the third person, as in 'he does'
kin are one's relatives or family

explanation.surface: Asking whether one's relatives produce fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' supplies DOES, the form it takes with a singular subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Doeskin is a soft fine woollen fabric with a smooth napped finish, as well as leather from a female deer.

clue.text: Upsetting Dan and Mary Carter

indicators.note: upsetting knocks things over and out of order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Two people, Dan and Mary, annoying someone called Carter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carter' looks like a surname; here it is a person who drives a cart.
explanation.definitionFit: A drayman drives a dray, a low heavy cart, traditionally delivering beer for a brewery.
